sm: The host of Objectively Speaking welcomes Joel Trammell, author of The Chief Executive Operating System. Trammell says teaching naval nuclear students showed him that putting smart people together does not by itself make an organization run well, which pushed him toward learning to be a CEO. He explains that becoming CEO is like reaching base camp, because it is a very different job from other executive roles. He also says nonprofit and for-profit CEOs do similar work, except that nonprofit customers often are not the ones funding the organization. The host adds his own symphony versus soup kitchen comparison.

Trammell divides the CEO job into phases by headcount. A founder with fewer than about twenty-five people is effectively a project manager. He notes that ten people have forty-five possible conversations, while a hundred have almost five thousand, so complexity grows far faster than headcount. He says running a public company of four thousand felt much like running a private one of two hundred seventy, but the jump from twenty to two hundred seventy is dramatic. Of the five duties a CEO cannot delegate, he says owning the vision is most neglected. He describes his first law of business: provide value to customers, employees, and shareholders, and arbitrage value among them.

Trammell says sales, marketing, and product delivery form a second triangle of tension, and a CEO's job is to referee. He calls this the CEO tightrope and cites Boeing, which he says focused too much on shareholder value, and praises Satya Nadella. In audience questions, he names the firefighter CEO as the biggest first-timer mistake. He says the most important hiring trait is buying into the mission, vision, and values. He also says a meritocracy needs consistent, disciplined performance management, and that great CEOs are curious and open-minded.

Trammell likens the six functional areas to wheels on a vehicle and asks each quarter which is turning slowest. He argues great CEOs are made more than born, because those who fail usually lack knowledge of the job rather than intelligence or work ethic. The role is lonely, with no junior version to learn on. He describes his courses, which grew out of his time leading the Austin Technology Council, including a three-day master class at his ranch for eight to twelve CEOs. Asked about confidence versus caution, he says excessive caution is the bigger danger, since competitors keep improving.

Asked about Nvidia, Trammell says he would fault a board with no succession plan and a CEO with sixty direct reports. He says a board member's duty is to shareholders, and he would have pushed for something short of firing. On CEO pay, he says headline packages are mostly stock options of uncertain value, but he objects to large payouts for failed CEOs. On AI, he says it excels at math and programming, which are hard for humans, but not at work driven by emotion and relationships. He tells CEOs to treat AI like brilliant new graduates who need training, so an AI strategy is really a people strategy.

Trammell says that if AI gains go entirely to shareholders, competitors will share them with customers and employees and win. He says CEOs underestimate the weight and loneliness of the job, and recalls feeling relief when he no longer managed other people's money. On pay, he says incentive pay misunderstands knowledge work and gets gamed. He prefers paying a consistent percentage of market value, so equally qualified people in the same job earn the same.

Trammell says a company is a community, not a family, with the CEO as mayor and sheriff, because a community can remove people who do not fit. He calls business a search for truth. He recalls giving employees the same slides he had given the board, and quotes Ayn Rand that you cannot evade the consequences of evading reality. He describes his Chat CEO tool, which draws on his system and the ideas of thinkers like Drucker and Deming, and which advises CEOs around the clock. He closes with a question about founders and CEOs, saying founders are rewarded for building and selling.

Trammell says that at about one hundred fifty employees a CEO must hire experts and coach them, and founders who will not let go stall the business. He disagrees with the idea of one correct leadership style, saying servant leadership is right only sometimes. He applies CEO principles to presidents and governors, suggesting a president drop party affiliation and fly to states with lawmakers, and says senators are poor training for the presidency. He says a CEO takes blame for failures and gives the team credit for successes. He wants to keep CEOs from failing and mentions his LinkedIn, his Substack Managing the Future, and Expert Loops. The host previews a webinar by Stephen Hicks on the Enlightenment.
